decks.title: Measurement of National Income — Part 1: Value Added and Income Methods
goals: Explain the three phases at which national income can be measured
Calculate value of output, gross value added and net value added at factor cost, and avoid double counting
Calculate domestic income and national income by the income method

slides.heading: Measurement of National Income
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the **value-added (product) method** and the **income method**.

nodes.label: Value of output and value added

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: three ways to measure national income, value of output and value added, double counting, the income method, and why the three totals agree
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: How does a country add up everything it produces in a year? Statisticians can count what is produced, what is earned, or what is spent. In this part we learn the first two ways: adding the value that each producer adds, and adding the incomes that production creates.

slides.heading: One flow, three phases
slides.body_md: National income can be measured where it is **produced**, where it is **distributed** as factor incomes, and where it is **spent**.

visual.alt: Flow of the three phases at which national income is measured: production by the product method, distribution of factor incomes by the income method, and disposition as final spending by the expenditure method
visual.caption: Three phases, three methods

slides.narration: Production, income and spending are three points on the same circular flow. Counting value added measures production. Adding wages, rent, interest, profit and mixed income measures distribution. Adding final spending measures disposition. Done carefully, all three give the same total.

slides.heading: Key terms of the product method
slides.body_md: Value added is what a producer **adds** to the inputs it buys.

rows: Market value of all goods made by a firm in the year
Closing stock − opening stock (can be negative)
Inputs bought from other producers and used up in the year
Gross value added at market price
What the firm adds to its inputs
Net value added at factor cost
Value added paid out to factors
GVA at market price − depreciation − net indirect taxes

visual.alt: Table of product-method terms: value of output equals sales plus change in stock; intermediate consumption is inputs used up; gross value added at market price is value of output minus intermediate consumption; net value added at factor cost subtracts depreciation and net indirect taxes

slides.narration: Start with the value of output: sales plus the change in stock. From it, subtract intermediate consumption, the inputs bought and used up during the year. What remains is gross value added at market price. Taking away depreciation and net indirect taxes gives net value added at factor cost, the part paid out to the factors.

slides.heading: Quick check: how much was double counted?
slides.body_md: A clerk adds the sales of cane, jaggery and sweets in a chain. By how much does he overstate final output?
slides.narration: Ask yourself which sales are of goods that end up inside other goods.

slides.heading: A chain of production
slides.body_md: Each stage adds value; the values added together equal the **final output**.

rows: Sweet shop sells sweets to households

visual.alt: Table of the imagined Mandya sweets chain: cane sold for 300, jaggery for 500 and sweets for 800 crore rupees; value added is 300, 200 and 300, totalling 800, the value of the sweets, while the sum of sales is 1,600
visual.caption: Imagined figures: adding sales counts the cane and jaggery again.

slides.narration: In this imagined chain, cane worth three hundred crore becomes jaggery worth five hundred, and then sweets worth eight hundred. The grower adds three hundred, the jaggery unit adds two hundred and the sweet shop adds three hundred. Together that is eight hundred, exactly the value of the sweets households buy.

slides.heading: Double counting and how to avoid it
slides.body_md: Adding every sale counts inputs **again**. Count either **final goods only** or **value added only**.

nodes.label: Inputs counted again inside later sales
Fix: final goods only, or value added only

visual.alt: Flow of double counting: adding every firm's full sales counts inputs again inside later sales, overstating output; the fix is to count final goods only or value added only
visual.caption: Double counting and its cure

slides.narration: If we simply add the sales of every firm, the cane is counted three times and the jaggery twice, because each is already inside the price of the next product. This error is called double counting. We avoid it either by counting only final goods and services, or by adding only the value that each firm adds.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: one firm, from sales to net value added
slides.body_md: An imagined pump maker in Pune: find its net value added at factor cost.
bullets: Step 1 — Change in stock is closing minus opening; here it is negative.
Step 2 — Value of output = sales + change in stock.
Step 3 — Subtract raw materials and power, but not the new machine.
Step 4 — Subtract depreciation, then net indirect taxes.

visual.alt: Worked table for an imagined Pune pump maker: a fall in stock of 100 gives value of output 2,300 lakh rupees; inputs of 1,300 give gross value added 1,000; less depreciation 90 and net indirect taxes 60 gives net value added at factor cost of 850
visual.caption: Imagined figures (₹ lakh).

slides.narration: The pump maker sold two thousand four hundred lakh of pumps, but its stock fell by one hundred, so this year's output was two thousand three hundred. Its inputs of raw materials and power were one thousand three hundred, so gross value added is one thousand. The new machine is a capital good, not an input. Removing depreciation and net indirect taxes leaves eight hundred and fifty lakh.

slides.heading: Quick check: a machine is not an input
slides.body_md: Find the pump maker's gross value added at market price.
slides.narration: Remember which purchases are used up in the year and which last for many years.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a four-firm chain
slides.body_md: Find the value added of each unit in the imagined Vidarbha cotton chain and of the chain as a whole.
bullets: Step 1 — For each unit, value of output = sales + change in stock.
Step 2 — Subtract the input bought from the unit before it.
Step 3 — Add the four values added.
Step 4 — Compare with the sum of values of output to see the double counting.

visual.alt: Table of the imagined Vidarbha cotton chain: values of output 400, 680, 980 and 1,550 lakh rupees; gross value added 340, 280, 330 and 550, totalling 1,500, against 3,610 if every value of output were added
visual.caption: Imagined figures (₹ lakh).

slides.narration: Work unit by unit. The ginning unit adds thirty lakh to its stock, so its output is six hundred and eighty, and after buying cotton for four hundred it adds two hundred and eighty. The spinning mill's stock falls, so its output is less than its sales. The four values added total one thousand five hundred lakh, far below the three thousand six hundred and ten got by adding every output.

slides.heading: The income method: three parts of domestic income
slides.body_md: Domestic income = **compensation of employees + operating surplus + mixed income**.

rows: Wages and salaries in cash and kind; employer's social security contributions
A nurse's salary and free housing
Rent and royalty; interest; profit (corporation tax, dividends, undistributed profit)
Interest earned on a loan to a factory
Earnings that combine several factor rewards
A tailor working in her own shop

visual.alt: Table of the three parts of domestic income under the income method: compensation of employees, operating surplus (rent, interest and profit) and mixed income of the self-employed, with an example of each

slides.narration: The income method adds the incomes that production pays out. Employees receive compensation. Owners of land, capital and enterprise receive the operating surplus: rent, interest and profit. The self-employed, who use their own labour and capital, earn mixed income. Together these give domestic income, and adding net factor income from abroad gives national income.

slides.heading: What counts as compensation of employees
slides.body_md: Rewards for work in **cash or kind**, plus the employer's **social security** contributions.

rows: Interest-free loans to staff (to be repaid)
Free meals, housing, uniforms (payments in kind)
Travel allowance for official tours (an input of the firm)
Employer's contribution to provident fund and health insurance

visual.alt: Table of what is and is not compensation of employees: wages, payments in kind and employer contributions are included; repayable staff loans, official travel costs and government pensions are not

slides.narration: Compensation of employees is more than the pay cheque. Free meals, housing or uniforms are rewards paid in kind, and the employer's share of provident fund or insurance contributions also counts. But a loan that staff must repay is not income, and costs of official tours are the firm's own expenses.

slides.heading: Quick check: meals and housing for nurses
slides.body_md: A hospital gives its nurses free meals and rent-free housing. How are these treated?
slides.narration: Ask whether the nurses receive these because they work.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: national income by the income method
slides.body_md: Imagined Suvarnagiri: build each part, add, then adjust for factor income from abroad.
bullets: Step 1 — Compensation of employees = wages + employer contributions.
Step 2 — Profit = corporation tax + dividends + undistributed profit.
Step 3 — Operating surplus = rent + interest + profit; add mixed income.
Step 4 — Add net factor income from abroad; leave out transfers.

visual.alt: Worked table for imagined Suvarnagiri: compensation of employees 1,590, profit 520, operating surplus 890, domestic income 3,090 and national income 3,115 crore rupees, with interest on national debt and scholarships left out as transfers
visual.caption: Imagined figures (₹ crore).

slides.narration: Wages and employer contributions give compensation of one thousand five hundred and ninety crore. Corporation tax, dividends and retained profit make a profit of five hundred and twenty, so the operating surplus is eight hundred and ninety. Adding mixed income gives domestic income of three thousand and ninety, and with factor income from abroad, national income is three thousand one hundred and fifteen. Interest on public debt and scholarships stay out.

slides.heading: Quick check: profit as the remainder
slides.body_md: Find profit when domestic income and the other factor incomes are known.
slides.narration: Subtract every other part of domestic income from the total.

slides.heading: Three methods, one total
slides.body_md: Value added, factor incomes and final spending all equal **₹800 crore** in the Mandya chain.

visual.caption: Imagined figures (₹ crore): the same flow measured at production, income and spending.

slides.narration: Here are the three measurements side by side. The values added by the grower, the jaggery unit and the sweet shop make eight hundred crore. The wages, rent, interest and profit they pay make eight hundred. And households spend eight hundred on sweets. Value added is paid out as income, and income is spent on the final output.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: National income can be measured at **production, distribution and disposition**.
Value added = value of output − intermediate consumption; this avoids **double counting**.
Domestic income = **compensation of employees + operating surplus + mixed income**.
National income = domestic income + **net factor income from abroad**.

rows: Value of output = sales + change in stock
GVA = value of output − intermediate consumption
NVA at factor cost: less depreciation and net indirect taxes
Add net factor income from abroad for national income

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: product method from value of output to net value added at factor cost, and income method from compensation of employees, operating surplus and mixed income to national income

slides.narration: To sum up, the product method adds the value each producer adds, never the full sales of every firm. The income method adds compensation of employees, operating surplus and mixed income, then adjusts for factor income from abroad. Both measure the same flow, so both must reach the same total.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always find **value of output** first: sales plus change in stock, with the sign of the change.
A **machine** bought is not intermediate consumption; only inputs used up in the year are.
Build **profit** from its parts before adding operating surplus.
Write the reason for every item you **leave out**, such as transfers or repayable loans.
slides.narration: Four habits earn marks. Begin with value of output and watch the sign of the change in stock. Do not subtract machines as inputs. In the income method, add corporation tax, dividends and undistributed profit before forming the operating surplus. And whenever you leave an item out, state why in a few words.

decks.title: Measurement of National Income — Part 2: Expenditure Method, Precautions and Difficulties
goals: Calculate GDP at market price and national income by the expenditure method
State and explain the precautions of each method, with the treatment of tricky items
Explain the difficulties of measuring national income in India

slides.heading: The Expenditure Method and Its Precautions
slides.body_md: Part 2 — measuring national income by **final spending**, and the care each method needs.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: final expenditure, capital formation and net exports, from gross domestic product to national income, precautions, and difficulties in India
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In this part we measure national income at the point where it is spent. We add the final spending of households, the government, producers and the rest of the world. Then we learn the precautions each method needs and why measurement is especially hard in India.

slides.heading: Four kinds of final expenditure
slides.body_md: GDP at market price = private and government final consumption + gross domestic capital formation + net exports.

rows: Households and non-profit bodies serving them
A new kiln; a rise in unsold stock
Exports of tea less imports of oil

visual.alt: Table of the four components of final expenditure: private and government final consumption, gross domestic capital formation and net exports, with who spends and an example of each

slides.narration: Households buy consumer goods and services. The government spends on the services it provides, such as schools and hospitals. Producers spend on new machines, buildings and stocks. And foreigners buy our exports, while we buy imports. Adding consumption, capital formation and exports, and taking away imports, gives gross domestic product at market price.

slides.heading: Capital formation and net exports
slides.body_md: Capital formation includes the **change in stock**; net exports can be **negative**.

nodes.label: minus depreciation gives net capital formation

visual.alt: Flow: gross domestic fixed capital formation plus change in stock equals gross domestic capital formation; minus depreciation gives net capital formation
visual.caption: Investment spending

slides.narration: Investment spending has two parts: new fixed assets, and the change in stocks of raw materials and finished goods. If stocks fall, the change is negative and lowers the total. Net exports are exports minus imports. When a country imports more than it exports, net exports are negative and reduce domestic product.

slides.heading: Quick check: GDP at market price
slides.body_md: Add the components for imagined Tamrapatna, taking care with the signs.
slides.narration: Watch the sign of the change in stock and remember to subtract imports.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: from final spending to national income
slides.body_md: Imagined Tamrapatna: find GDP at market price, GNP at market price and national income.
bullets: Step 1 — Capital formation = fixed capital formation + change in stock.
Step 2 — Net exports = exports − imports.
Step 3 — Add the four components: GDP at market price.
Step 4 — Subtract depreciation and net indirect taxes; add net factor income from abroad.

visual.alt: Worked table for imagined Tamrapatna: capital formation 780 and net exports minus 50 give GDP at market price 4,580 crore rupees; GNP at market price is 4,545; net domestic product at factor cost 4,140; national income 4,105
visual.caption: Imagined figures (₹ crore).

slides.narration: Fixed capital formation of eight hundred and twenty and a fall in stock of forty give capital formation of seven hundred and eighty. Exports of three hundred and sixty less imports of four hundred and ten give net exports of minus fifty. Gross domestic product at market price is four thousand five hundred and eighty crore. After depreciation, net indirect taxes and a negative factor income from abroad, national income is four thousand one hundred and five.

slides.heading: Steps of the expenditure method
slides.body_md: Identify, classify, estimate and add, then adjust.

nodes.label: Estimate and add: GDP at market price

visual.alt: Flow of the steps of the expenditure method: identify the units making final expenditure, classify it, estimate and add to get GDP at market price, then adjust to national income
visual.caption: Expenditure method in four steps

slides.narration: First identify all the units that make final expenditure. Next classify their spending into consumption, capital formation and net exports. Estimate each class and add them to get gross domestic product at market price. Finally subtract depreciation and net indirect taxes, and add net factor income from abroad, to reach national income.

slides.heading: Quick check: a fall in stock
slides.body_md: Find gross domestic capital formation when stocks fall during the year.
slides.narration: A fall in stock is a negative change in stock.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: sorting a mixed list
slides.body_md: Imagined Shivgarh gives eight items. Decide which to add, which to subtract and which to leave out.
bullets: Step 1 — Add consumption, government consumption, capital formation and exports.
Step 2 — Subtract imports.
Step 3 — Leave out pensions, shares and second-hand buses, with reasons.
Step 4 — State the total with its unit.

visual.alt: Worked table for imagined Shivgarh: consumption 960, government consumption 240, capital formation 300 and exports 70 are added, imports 90 subtracted, and pensions, shares and second-hand buses left out, giving GDP at market price of 1,480 crore rupees
visual.caption: Imagined figures (₹ crore).

slides.narration: Exam tables often hide items that do not belong. Here we add consumption, government consumption, capital formation and exports, and subtract imports, to get one thousand four hundred and eighty crore. Pensions are transfers, shares are financial assets, and second-hand buses were counted when they were new, so all three are left out.

slides.heading: Precautions: value-added method
slides.body_md: Avoid double counting, and remember the goods that are produced but never sold.

rows: Inputs are already inside the value of later output
Leave out sales of second-hand goods; count the commission
The good was counted when new; the dealer's service is new
It is output of the year even if not sold
Include imputed rent of owner-occupied houses
A housing service is produced and used

visual.alt: Table of precautions for the value-added method: avoid double counting, leave out second-hand sales but count commissions, include production for self-consumption and imputed rent, with a reason for each

slides.narration: In the value-added method, the main danger is double counting, so only value added is counted. Second-hand goods are left out, though a dealer's commission is new output. Food a farmer keeps for his family, and the housing service of an owner-occupied home, are produced in the year and are valued and included.

slides.heading: Precautions: income method
slides.body_md: Count only incomes **earned in production**.

rows: No factor service is supplied in return
Leave out windfall gains such as lottery prizes
They are not earned in production
Leave out capital gains on selling old assets
Include payments in kind and imputed incomes

visual.alt: Table of precautions for the income method: leave out transfers, windfall gains and capital gains, and include payments in kind and imputed incomes, with a reason for each

slides.narration: In the income method, include only incomes earned by supplying factor services. Pensions, scholarships and other transfers are left out. So are lottery prizes and gains from selling old property, because nothing new is produced. Payments in kind and imputed incomes, such as the rent of an owner-occupied house, are included.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the treatment
slides.body_md: Match each transaction with how it is treated in national income.
slides.narration: For each one, ask whether anything new was produced in the year.

slides.heading: Precautions: expenditure method
slides.body_md: Count **final** spending only; leave out second-hand goods, financial assets and transfers.

rows: Spending on intermediate goods is already in final goods
Leave out spending on second-hand goods
The goods were counted when first produced
Leave out purchases of shares and bonds
They are financial assets, not goods or services
Leave out transfer payments by government
The receivers' own spending is counted instead

visual.alt: Table of precautions for the expenditure method: count final expenditure only and leave out second-hand goods, financial assets and transfer payments, with a reason for each

slides.narration: In the expenditure method, count only spending on final goods and services, because intermediate goods are already inside them. Spending on second-hand goods, on shares and bonds, and on transfer payments such as pensions is left out. Otherwise the same output would be counted twice, or something that is not output would be counted.

slides.heading: Difficulties in measuring national income in India
slides.body_md: Indian figures are careful **estimates**, not exact counts.

nodes.label: Large non-monetised sector: output kept for self-use or bartered
Many small producers keep no accounts
Incomes under-reported in the informal sector
Estimates rely on samples and assumptions

visual.alt: Flow of difficulties in measuring national income in India: a large non-monetised sector, small producers without accounts, under-reported informal incomes, and estimates that rely on samples and assumptions
visual.caption: Why the figures are estimates

slides.narration: Measurement is hard in India for several reasons. Much farm output is kept for home use or exchanged without money, so its value must be estimated. Many small producers and self-employed workers keep no accounts, and some incomes go unreported. So statisticians rely on surveys, samples and assumptions to complete the picture.

slides.heading: Quick check: a lottery prize
slides.body_md: True or false: a lottery prize is included in national income.
slides.narration: Ask whether the prize rewards any productive service.

slides.heading: Comparing the three methods
columns:
**Where each measures**

- Value added: production
- Income: distribution
- Expenditure: disposition

**Main danger**

- Value added: double counting
- Income: counting transfers
- Expenditure: counting non-final spending

rows: Compensation of employees + operating surplus + mixed income

visual.alt: Comparison table of the three methods: value added measured at production with double counting avoided; income measured at distribution with transfers left out; expenditure measured at disposition with only final spending counted

slides.narration: Each method looks at a different phase of the same flow. The value-added method measures production and must avoid double counting. The income method measures distribution and must keep out transfers. The expenditure method measures disposition and must count only final spending. In practice, statisticians use all three to check one another.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: GDP at market price = private and government final consumption + capital formation + **net exports**.
National income = GDP at market price − depreciation − net indirect taxes + net factor income from abroad.
Leave out **transfers, second-hand goods and financial assets**; include imputed rent and self-consumption.
In India, **non-monetised output** and **missing data** make the figures estimates.

rows: No second-hand goods, shares or transfers
Non-monetised output and missing data in India

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: the components of final expenditure and adjustment to national income, beside the main precautions and the difficulties of measurement in India

slides.narration: To sum up, the expenditure method adds final spending and then adjusts to national income. Every method needs care: transfers, second-hand goods and financial assets stay out, while imputed rent and production for self-use come in. And in India, much output is never bought or sold, so national income is always an estimate.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Set out workings in **steps**, naming each aggregate as you reach it.
Use the **sign** of net exports, change in stock and net factor income exactly as given.
In "treatment" questions, say **included or excluded** and give **one reason**.
Commission on second-hand goods and brokerage on shares are **included**.
slides.narration: Four points to remember. Show each step and name the aggregate you reach. Keep every sign as given, especially negative net exports, a fall in stock or negative factor income from abroad. In treatment questions, state the decision and the reason. And remember that commissions and brokerage are payments for services, so they are included.

notes.title: Measurement of National Income — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Three phases, three methods
sections.body_md:
- National income is generated in **production**, **distributed** as factor incomes and **disposed of** as spending. It can be measured at each phase.
- **Product (value-added) method** at production; **income method** at distribution; **expenditure method** at disposition.
- Because value added is paid out as incomes and incomes are spent on final output, the three totals are equal when measured correctly.

key_terms.definition_md: Measures national income as the sum of the values added by all producing units.
Measures national income as the sum of factor incomes earned in production.
Measures national income as the sum of final expenditure on domestic output, adjusted to factor cost and national.

sections.heading: 2. The value-added (product) method
sections.body_md:
- **Value of output** = sales + change in stock (closing stock − opening stock).
- **Intermediate consumption**: goods and services bought from other producers and used up in the year (raw materials, power, fuel, repairs). Machines and buildings are **not** intermediate consumption.
- **Gross value added at market price** = value of output − intermediate consumption.
- **Net value added at factor cost** = GVA at market price − depreciation − net indirect taxes (indirect taxes − subsidies).
- Sum of GVA of all units = GDP at market price; adjust to national income in the usual way.

sections.heading: 3. Double counting
sections.body_md:
- **Double counting** means counting the value of the same input more than once, which overstates output.
- It happens when the full sales of every firm in a chain are added.
- Two cures: (1) the **final product approach**, counting only final goods and services; (2) the **value-added approach**, counting only what each firm adds.

sections.heading: 4. The income method
sections.body_md:
- **Compensation of employees**: wages and salaries in cash and kind, and the employer's contributions to social security schemes.
- **Operating surplus**: rent and royalty, interest, and profit (corporation tax + dividends + undistributed profit).
- **Mixed income of the self-employed**: earnings that combine several factor rewards, such as those of farmers, artisans and small traders.
- Domestic income (NDP at factor cost) = compensation of employees + operating surplus + mixed income. National income = domestic income + net factor income from abroad.
- Steps: identify producing units and group them into sectors; classify and estimate their factor payments; add; adjust for factor income from abroad.

sections.heading: 5. The expenditure method
sections.body_md:
- **Final expenditure** on domestic output: private final consumption expenditure; government final consumption expenditure; gross domestic capital formation (gross fixed capital formation + change in stock); net exports (exports − imports).
- Their sum is **GDP at market price**. National income = GDP at market price − consumption of fixed capital − net indirect taxes + net factor income from abroad.
- Imports are subtracted because they are produced outside the domestic territory.
- Steps: identify the units making final expenditure; classify it; estimate and add; adjust to national income.

sections.heading: 6. Precautions and difficulties
sections.body_md:
- **Value-added method**: avoid double counting; exclude sales of second-hand goods but include commissions on them; include production for self-consumption and imputed rent of owner-occupied houses.
- **Income method**: exclude transfer payments (pensions, scholarships, unemployment allowance, interest on national debt), windfall gains and capital gains; include payments in kind and imputed incomes; repayable loans to staff are not income.
- **Expenditure method**: count final expenditure only; exclude spending on second-hand goods, financial assets (shares, bonds) and transfer payments; include brokerage on financial assets.
- **Unpaid services** at home are left out by convention, though they are valuable.
- **Difficulties in India**: a large non-monetised sector; many small producers without accounts; under-reported informal incomes; difficulty of valuing depreciation and self-consumption; reliance on surveys and samples.

questions.stem_md: A student summarising the product method for her Class 12 notes in Nagpur must write the correct formula for gross value added at market price. Which is it?

options.text_md: Sales minus wages paid to workers
Value of output minus intermediate consumption
Value of output plus intermediate consumption
Sales minus purchase of machines

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Value of output minus intermediate consumption. Gross value added at market price is what the firm adds to the inputs it buys: value of output less intermediate consumption. Wages are part of value added, not a deduction; adding inputs counts them twice; machines are capital goods, not inputs used up.

questions.stem_md: When a firm makes more goods in a year than it sells, which expression gives its value of output?

options.text_md: Sales minus the change in stock
Sales only
Closing stock only
Sales plus the change in stock

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Sales plus the change in stock. Unsold goods made this year are added to stock, and they are part of this year's production. So the change in stock (closing minus opening) is added to sales; sales alone would miss these goods.

questions.stem_md: For an imagined bus company in Mangaluru, which purchase is part of its intermediate consumption in the year?

options.text_md: Diesel used to run the buses
A new bus bought for the route to Udupi
Shares of an oil company
Land bought for a new depot

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Diesel used to run the buses. Intermediate consumption is goods and services used up within the year in producing output, such as fuel. A bus is a capital good lasting many years, shares are a financial asset, and land is not produced in the year.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined Mandya sweets chain, a cane grower sells cane worth ₹300 crore to a jaggery unit, which sells jaggery worth ₹500 crore to a sweet shop, which sells sweets worth ₹800 crore to households. A clerk adds all three sales. By how much has he overstated the value of final output?

options.text_md: ₹1600 crore
₹500 crore
₹800 crore
₹300 crore

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹800 crore. Adding the sales gives 300 + 500 + 800 = 1600, but final output is only the sweets, worth 800. The overstatement is 1600 − 800 = ₹800 crore, the value of the cane and jaggery counted again inside the sweets.

questions.stem_md: An imagined pump maker in Pune sold goods worth ₹2,400 lakh. Its stock of finished pumps fell from ₹250 lakh to ₹150 lakh. What was its value of output?

options.text_md: ₹2,500 lakh
₹2,400 lakh
₹2,300 lakh
₹2,250 lakh

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹2,300 lakh. Change in stock = 150 − 250 = −100. Value of output = 2,400 − 100 = ₹2,300 lakh: part of the year's sales came from pumps made in earlier years.

questions.stem_md: Why is a lathe bought by an imagined workshop in Rajkot not deducted as intermediate consumption when its value added is found?

options.text_md: It is a capital good used over many years, not used up in the year's production
It was bought from another country
It is paid for out of the owner's savings
Machines never wear out

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It is a capital good used over many years, not used up in the year's production. Intermediate consumption covers inputs used up within the year. A lathe is a fixed asset; only its wear and tear (depreciation) is deducted, and that is done when moving from gross to net value added.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Under the product method, only the value of final goods, or the sum of values added, is counted as national output.

**Reason (R):** The value of intermediate goods is already included in the price of the final goods made from them.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: counting intermediate goods separately would add their value a second time, which is double counting.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Adding up the sales of every firm along a chain of production overstates the value of the final output of that chain.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** True. Each firm's sales include the value of inputs bought from the firm before it, so the inputs are counted more than once. This is the problem of double counting.

questions.stem_md: Goods and services bought from other producers and used up during the year in producing output are called ___ consumption.
questions.solution_md: They are intermediate consumption; subtracting them from the value of output gives value added.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined Mandya sweets chain (cane ₹300 crore, jaggery ₹500 crore, sweets ₹800 crore; the grower buys no inputs), find the total value added (in ₹ crore).
questions.solution_md: Value added: grower 300, jaggery unit 500 − 300 = 200, sweet shop 800 − 500 = 300. Total = 300 + 200 + 300 = 800, that is ₹800 crore.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Pune pump maker has sales ₹2,400 lakh, a fall in stock of ₹100 lakh, raw materials ₹1,100 lakh and power ₹200 lakh. It also bought a machine for ₹300 lakh. Find its gross value added at market price (in ₹ lakh).
questions.solution_md: Value of output = 2,400 − 100 = 2,300. Intermediate consumption = 1,100 + 200 = 1,300 (the machine is a capital good, not an input). GVA = 2,300 − 1,300 = 1,000, that is ₹1,000 lakh.

questions.stem_md: Explain double counting with an example from a chain that turns raw silk into saris.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, then an example showing the repeated input.

answer.model_answer_md: **Double counting** means counting the value of an input more than once. If a weaver's sale of silk yarn to a sari maker is added to the sari maker's sale of saris, the **yarn is counted twice**, because its value is already inside the price of the saris.

questions.stem_md: State two ways of avoiding double counting when national output is measured.
questions.solution_md: Final product approach and value-added approach.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Final product approach**: count only the value of **final goods and services**, leaving out goods bought for further production.
2. **Value-added approach**: add only the **value added** by each firm, that is, value of output minus intermediate consumption.

questions.stem_md: Find the net value added at factor cost of an imagined Pune pump maker (₹ lakh): sales 2,400; opening stock 250; closing stock 150; raw materials 1,100; power and fuel 200; new machine bought 300; depreciation 90; net indirect taxes 60.
questions.solution_md: Value of output, inputs (not the machine), then depreciation and net indirect taxes.

answer.model_answer_md: Change in stock = 150 − 250 = −100, so value of output = 2,400 − 100 = **2,300**. Intermediate consumption = 1,100 + 200 = **1,300**; the machine is a **capital good** and is left out. Gross value added at market price = 2,300 − 1,300 = 1,000. Net value added at factor cost = 1,000 − 90 − 60 = **₹850 lakh**.

questions.stem_md: An imagined ginning unit in Vidarbha sold lint worth ₹650 lakh, added ₹30 lakh to its stock and bought raw cotton for ₹400 lakh. A spinning mill sold yarn worth ₹1,000 lakh, ran down its stock by ₹20 lakh and bought lint for ₹650 lakh. Find the gross value added of each unit and explain why the two sales are not simply added.
questions.solution_md: Value of output and value added for each unit; reason against adding sales.

answer.model_answer_md: Ginning unit: value of output = 650 + 30 = 680; GVA = 680 − 400 = **₹280 lakh**. Spinning mill: value of output = 1,000 − 20 = 980; GVA = 980 − 650 = **₹330 lakh**. The mill's yarn already contains the lint it bought, so adding both sales would count the lint **twice**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about the imagined Vidarbha cotton chain (₹ lakh). [3 + 2]

| Unit | Sales | Change in stock | Intermediate consumption |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cotton farm | 400 | 0 | 60 |
| Ginning unit | 650 | 30 | 400 |
| Spinning mill | 1,000 | -20 | 650 |
| Garment unit | 1,500 | 50 | 1,000 |

(a) Find the gross value added of each unit and of the whole chain. [3]
(b) The garment unit's depreciation is ₹40 lakh, it pays indirect taxes of ₹45 lakh and receives a subsidy of ₹15 lakh. Find its net value added at factor cost. [2]
questions.solution_md: Value of output and value added for each unit, the chain total, then the factor-cost net figure.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Value of output = sales + change in stock; gross value added = value of output − intermediate consumption.
- Cotton farm: 400 + (0) = 400; 400 − 60 = **340**
- Ginning unit: 650 + (30) = 680; 680 − 400 = **280**
- Spinning mill: 1,000 + (-20) = 980; 980 − 650 = **330**
- Garment unit: 1,500 + (50) = 1,550; 1,550 − 1,000 = **550**
Total gross value added of the chain = 340 + 280 + 330 + 550 = **₹1,500 lakh**, far less than the ₹3,610 lakh got by adding every value of output, because that sum repeats the inputs.
(b) Net indirect taxes = 45 − 15 = 30. Net value added at factor cost = 550 − 40 − 30 = **₹480 lakh**.

questions.stem_md: An imagined textile company in Coimbatore pays wages, pays its share of contributions to employees' provident fund and gives workers free uniforms. Under the income method, all three are counted as

options.text_md: operating surplus
mixed income of the self-employed
transfer payments
compensation of employees

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** compensation of employees. Compensation of employees covers wages and salaries in cash, payments in kind such as free uniforms, and the employer's contribution to social security schemes such as provident fund. None is rent, interest or profit, and none is a transfer.

questions.stem_md: Which group of incomes together makes up operating surplus in the income method?

options.text_md: Wages, salaries and bonus
Rent and royalty, interest and profit
Pensions, scholarships and subsidies
Wages and mixed income

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Rent and royalty, interest and profit. Operating surplus is the income from property and enterprise: rent and royalty, interest and profit. Wages belong to compensation of employees; pensions and scholarships are transfers.

questions.stem_md: A carpenter in an imagined village near Hubballi works in his own shed with his own tools and sells furniture. His earnings are recorded under the income method as

options.text_md: mixed income of the self-employed
compensation of employees
rent and royalty
interest

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** mixed income of the self-employed. He supplies his own labour, building and tools, so his earnings mix wages, rent, interest and profit that cannot be separated easily. Such earnings are recorded as mixed income of the self-employed.

questions.stem_md: A listed company in an imagined industrial town divides its year's profit into three uses. Which list gives those three parts as used in the income method?

options.text_md: Wages, rent and interest
Corporation tax, dividends and undistributed profit
Depreciation, indirect taxes and subsidies
Dividends, bonus shares and loans

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Corporation tax, dividends and undistributed profit. Profit is either paid to the government as corporation tax, paid to shareholders as dividends, or kept in the business as undistributed (retained) profit. Wages, rent and interest are other factor incomes; depreciation and indirect taxes are not profit.

questions.stem_md: Which of these receipts of a family in an imagined town in Odisha is NOT a factor income?

options.text_md: Rent received for a shop let out in the market
Salary earned by the father as a bank clerk
A scholarship received by the daughter from the state government
Interest received on a fixed deposit with a bank

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A scholarship received by the daughter from the state government. A scholarship is a transfer payment: nothing is produced in return. Rent, salary and interest on a deposit lent to a bank are rewards for factor services and are factor incomes.

questions.stem_md: An imagined hospital in Lucknow provides free meals and rent-free housing to its nurses. How are these treated in the income method?

options.text_md: Excluded, because no money is paid
Included in operating surplus of the hospital
Treated as transfer payments to the nurses
Included in compensation of employees as payments in kind

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Included in compensation of employees as payments in kind. Meals and housing given to employees are a reward for their work, paid in kind instead of cash, so they are valued and included in compensation of employees.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Interest paid by the government on the national debt is excluded from domestic income.

**Reason (R):** Such interest is treated as a transfer payment, because government loans are taken largely for non-productive purposes.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: since the borrowed funds are not treated as having produced income, the interest is recorded as a transfer and kept out of domestic income.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Mixed income of the self-employed is left out when domestic income is found by the income method.

**Reason (R):** Self-employed persons do not contribute to the production of goods and services.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are false. Mixed income is one of the three parts of domestic income under the income method, and the self-employed, such as farmers, artisans and shopkeepers, do produce goods and services.

questions.stem_md: Rent, interest and profit together are called operating ___ in the income method.
questions.solution_md: They make up the operating surplus, the income from property and entrepreneurship.

questions.stem_md: In imagined Suvarnagiri, wages and salaries are ₹1,450 crore and employers' contributions to social security schemes are ₹140 crore. Firms also gave interest-free loans of ₹45 crore to staff. Find compensation of employees (in ₹ crore).
questions.solution_md: Compensation of employees = 1,450 + 140 = 1,590, that is ₹1,590 crore. An interest-free loan must be repaid, so it is not a reward for work and is left out.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Konark has domestic income (NDP at factor cost) of ₹2,600 crore, compensation of employees ₹1,250 crore, rent ₹180 crore, interest ₹140 crore and mixed income ₹570 crore. Find profit (in ₹ crore).
Name the two main parts of compensation of employees and give one example of each from a hotel in Shimla.
questions.solution_md: Wages and salaries (cash and kind); employer's social security contributions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Wages and salaries in cash and kind**: monthly salary of a receptionist, or free meals given to the kitchen staff.
2. **Employer's contribution to social security**: the hotel's share of contributions to its workers' provident fund or health insurance.

questions.stem_md: What is operating surplus? Which three incomes does it contain?
questions.solution_md: Meaning and its three parts.

answer.model_answer_md: **Operating surplus** is the income from **property and entrepreneurship** earned in production. It is made up of **rent and royalty**, **interest** and **profit** (corporation tax, dividends and undistributed profit).

questions.stem_md: Find domestic income of imagined Suvarnagiri by the income method (₹ crore): wages and salaries 1,450; employers' social security contributions 140; rent and royalty 210; interest 160; corporation tax 90; dividends 230; undistributed profit 200; mixed income 610; interest on national debt 70; scholarships 40.
questions.solution_md: Compensation of employees, operating surplus, mixed income; transfers excluded.

answer.model_answer_md: Compensation of employees = 1,450 + 140 = **1,590**. Profit = 90 + 230 + 200 = 520, so operating surplus = 210 + 160 + 520 = **890**. Domestic income = 1,590 + 890 + 610 = **₹3,090 crore**. Interest on national debt and scholarships are **transfers** and are left out.

marking_scheme.step: Operating surplus with profit built up

questions.stem_md: Describe the steps followed in estimating national income by the income method.
questions.solution_md: Identify sectors; classify and estimate factor incomes; add and adjust for factor income from abroad.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Identify** the producing enterprises and group them into industrial sectors (primary, secondary, tertiary).
2. **Classify** the factor incomes they pay into compensation of employees, operating surplus and mixed income, and estimate each.
3. **Add** the three for every sector to get domestic income, then **add net factor income from abroad** to reach national income.

marking_scheme.step: Add, then add net factor income from abroad

questions.stem_md: A family in an imagined suburb of Hyderabad buys a refrigerator for its kitchen. In the expenditure method this purchase is part of

options.text_md: gross domestic capital formation
government final consumption expenditure
intermediate consumption
private final consumption expenditure

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** private final consumption expenditure. Households buying goods for their own use make private final consumption expenditure, even for durables such as a refrigerator. Capital formation is investment by producers; government spending is by the state; intermediate consumption is by firms.

questions.stem_md: Which spending by the government of an imagined state is counted as government final consumption expenditure?

options.text_md: Old-age pensions paid to retired farmers
Unemployment allowance paid to job seekers
Salaries of teachers in government schools
Interest paid on loans raised from the public

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Salaries of teachers in government schools. Teachers' salaries buy a service (teaching) that the government provides free to the public, so they are final consumption by the government. Pensions, allowances and interest on public debt are transfers with no service in return.

questions.stem_md: Gross domestic capital formation used in the expenditure method is made up of

options.text_md: private and government consumption expenditure
gross domestic fixed capital formation and change in stock
exports and imports
depreciation and net indirect taxes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** gross domestic fixed capital formation and change in stock. Investment spending = additions to fixed assets (gross fixed capital formation) + change in stock (inventory investment). Consumption and net exports are other parts of final expenditure; depreciation and taxes are adjustments.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Tamrapatna exports goods and services worth ₹360 crore and imports goods and services worth ₹410 crore. What is its net export, and what does it do to domestic product at market price?

options.text_md: ₹-50 crore; it lowers domestic product by ₹50 crore
₹50 crore; it raises domestic product by ₹50 crore
₹770 crore; it raises domestic product
Zero; trade does not affect domestic product

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹-50 crore; it lowers domestic product by ₹50 crore. Net exports = 360 − 410 = -50. A negative figure means part of home spending went on foreign output, so adding net exports reduces domestic product at market price by ₹50 crore.

questions.stem_md: A statistician in an imagined state is listing items for the expenditure method. Which item must she leave out?

options.text_md: Purchase of new tractors by farmers
Old-age pensions paid by the state government
Salaries of government doctors
Exports of handloom saris

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Old-age pensions paid by the state government. Old-age pensions are transfer payments; the spending of the pensioners is already counted when they buy goods. Tractors are capital formation, doctors' salaries are government final consumption and exports are part of net exports.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Tamrapatna (₹ crore): private final consumption 3,200; government final consumption 650; gross domestic fixed capital formation 820; change in stock -40; exports 360; imports 410. What is its gross domestic product at market price?

options.text_md: ₹4,660 crore
₹4,990 crore
₹4,630 crore
₹4,580 crore

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** ₹4,580 crore. GDP at market price = 3,200 + 650 + (820 − 40) + (360 − 410) = 3,200 + 650 + 780 + (-50) = 4,580, that is ₹4,580 crore. Treating the fall in stock as a rise gives 4,660; forgetting to subtract imports gives 4,990; leaving out net exports altogether gives 4,630.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Imports are subtracted when domestic product is estimated by the expenditure method.

**Reason (R):** Imports are usually paid for in foreign currency.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. Imports are subtracted because they are produced outside the domestic territory, so spending on them creates no domestic output; the currency used to pay for them is not the reason.

questions.stem_md: True or false? When a family in Indore buys a five-year-old car from a neighbour, the full price is added to private final consumption expenditure for the year.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. The car was produced and counted in the year it was made; buying it again only transfers an existing good. Only a dealer's commission, if any, is a new service and is counted.

questions.stem_md: In imagined Tamrapatna, gross domestic fixed capital formation is ₹820 crore and stocks fell by ₹40 crore during the year. Find gross domestic capital formation (in ₹ crore).
questions.solution_md: Gross domestic capital formation = 820 + (-40) = 780, that is ₹780 crore.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Kavalpur (₹ crore): private final consumption 1,800; government final consumption 400; gross domestic capital formation 500; net exports 60; consumption of fixed capital 120; net indirect taxes 140; net factor income from abroad 20. Find national income (in ₹ crore).
questions.solution_md: GDP at market price = 1,800 + 400 + 500 + 60 = 2,760. National income = 2,760 − 120 − 140 + 20 = 2,520, that is ₹2,520 crore.

marking_scheme.step: Gross domestic product at market price

questions.stem_md: What does gross domestic capital formation include? Give an example of each part from a cement company.
questions.solution_md: Fixed capital formation and change in stock, with examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Gross domestic fixed capital formation**: spending on new fixed assets, such as a new kiln or trucks bought by the cement company.
2. **Change in stock**: the rise in unsold cement bags and stored limestone over the year.

questions.stem_md: Why are net exports, and not total exports, added in the expenditure method? Explain with an example.
questions.solution_md: Exports add, imports subtract; net exports in an example.

answer.model_answer_md: Spending on domestic output includes **exports**, bought by foreigners, but home spending also buys **imports**, which are produced abroad. So imports are **subtracted**. For example, if a country exports ₹100 crore and imports ₹130 crore, net exports of −₹30 crore are added.

questions.stem_md: For imagined Tamrapatna (₹ crore), GDP at market price is 4,580, consumption of fixed capital 180, net indirect taxes 260 and net factor income from abroad -35. Find GNP at market price and national income, showing each step.
questions.solution_md: Add factor income from abroad for GNP; subtract depreciation and net indirect taxes for national income.

answer.model_answer_md: GNP at market price = GDP at market price + net factor income from abroad = 4,580 + (-35) = **₹4,545 crore**. NDP at market price = 4,580 − 180 = 4,400; NDP at factor cost = 4,400 − 260 = 4,140. National income = 4,140 + (-35) = **₹4,105 crore**.

marking_scheme.step: Net domestic product at factor cost

questions.stem_md: Describe the steps followed in estimating national income by the expenditure method.
questions.solution_md: Identify units; classify and add final expenditure; adjust to national income.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Identify** the economic units that make final expenditure: households, government, producers and the rest of the world.
2. **Classify and estimate** final expenditure as private and government final consumption, gross domestic capital formation and net exports; their sum is GDP at market price.
3. **Adjust**: subtract consumption of fixed capital and net indirect taxes, and add net factor income from abroad, to reach national income.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about imagined Tamrapatna (₹ crore). [3 + 2]

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Private final consumption expenditure | 3,200 |
| Government final consumption expenditure | 650 |
| Gross domestic fixed capital formation | 820 |
| Change in stock | -40 |

| Net indirect taxes | 260 |

(a) Calculate national income by the expenditure method. [3]
(b) Explain why one item in the table is not used, and state one other precaution of this method. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Gross domestic capital formation = 820 + (-40) = 780; net exports = 360 − 410 = -50.
GDP at market price = 3,200 + 650 + 780 + (-50) = **4,580**.

questions.stem_md: Why is an unemployment allowance paid by an imagined state government excluded from national income?

options.text_md: It is a transfer payment for which no good or service is produced
It is paid only to people living in cities
It is too small to affect the total
It is paid out of taxes collected last year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It is a transfer payment for which no good or service is produced. National income counts incomes earned in production. An allowance is received without supplying any factor service, so it is a transfer and is left out; where it is paid from, or its size, does not matter.

questions.stem_md: An investor in an imagined city buys shares of a cement company worth ₹2 lakh through a broker who charges ₹1,000. What is included in national income?

options.text_md: The full ₹2 lakh paid for the shares
₹2 lakh plus the ₹1,000 commission
Only the broker's commission of ₹1,000
Nothing at all

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Only the broker's commission of ₹1,000. Buying shares only changes who owns a financial asset; no good or service is produced, so the ₹2 lakh is left out. The broker provides a service in the year, so the commission is included.

questions.stem_md: A family in an imagined town in Kerala lives in a house it owns. How is the housing service it enjoys treated in national income?

options.text_md: It is excluded, because no rent is paid
The market value of the house is included every year
Its imputed rent is estimated and included
It is included only if the family takes a housing loan

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Its imputed rent is estimated and included. An owner-occupied house still provides a housing service. Its value is imputed at the rent a tenant would pay and included, so that national income does not change just because a house is owned rather than rented.

questions.stem_md: A farmer in an imagined village in Bihar keeps part of his rice harvest to feed his family. How is this rice treated?

options.text_md: It is valued at the market price and included as production for self-consumption
It is excluded because it is never sold
It is included only when the family sells it later
It is treated as a transfer from the farmer to his family

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It is valued at the market price and included as production for self-consumption. The rice is produced in the year whether sold or kept. Production for self-consumption is valued at market price and included in national income.

questions.stem_md: Cooking and cleaning done by a homemaker for her own family in an imagined Jaipur household are not counted in national income mainly because

options.text_md: they are not useful to the family
homemakers do not pay income tax
they are done for less than eight hours a day
they are difficult to value, as no market transaction takes place

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** they are difficult to value, as no market transaction takes place. These services are valuable, but they are not bought or sold, and estimating their value is very difficult, so by convention they are left out. This is one reason national income understates total production.

questions.stem_md: A dealer in an imagined town buys an old motorcycle for ₹40,000 and sells it a week later for ₹46,000. What is added to national income?

options.text_md: ₹46,000, the selling price
₹6,000, the dealer's margin for his service
₹86,000, both prices
Nothing, as the motorcycle is old

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ₹6,000, the dealer's margin for his service. The motorcycle was counted when it was first made, so its price is not counted again. The dealer's margin of ₹46,000 − ₹40,000 = ₹6,000 rewards a service produced this year and is included.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Vegetables grown by a family in its backyard and eaten at home are included in national income.

**Reason (R):** Only goods that are sold in the market are counted in national income.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: production for self-consumption is valued and included. R is false: if only marketed goods were counted, such output would be left out.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A lottery prize of ₹10 lakh won by a teacher in Kochi is included in national income because it adds to her income.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. A lottery prize is a windfall gain, not a reward for any productive service, so it is excluded from national income.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps a statistician in an imagined state follows to estimate national income by the expenditure method.

options.text_md: Classify final expenditure into consumption, capital formation and net exports
Subtract depreciation and net indirect taxes, then add net factor income from abroad
Identify the units that make final expenditure
Estimate and add the components to get GDP at market price

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (c) → (a) → (d) → (b). Units first, then the classes of final expenditure, then their total at market price, and last the adjustments that turn the total into national income.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Match each transaction in an imagined town with its correct treatment in national income.

options.text_md: Old-age pension paid by the state
Rent a family would pay for the flat it owns
Broker's fee on a sale of bonds
Purchase of bonds of a power company

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Pensions and financial assets create no new output; imputed rent and the broker's service are production of the year.

questions.stem_md: State two difficulties in measuring national income in India.
questions.solution_md: Any two: non-monetised output, lack of data or accounts, informal sector, illiteracy, unrecorded incomes.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Non-monetised sector**: much farm output is kept for self-consumption or bartered, so its value must be estimated.
2. **Lack of reliable data**: many small producers keep no accounts, so incomes and output in the informal sector are hard to record.

questions.stem_md: A firm gives its workers free bus passes and also gives them interest-free loans. Explain why one is part of national income and the other is not.
questions.solution_md: Payment in kind against a repayable loan.

answer.model_answer_md: **Free bus passes** are a reward for work paid in kind, so they are part of **compensation of employees** and included. An **interest-free loan** must be **repaid**; it is not a payment for any service, so it is not income and is excluded.

marking_scheme.step: Bus passes included as payment in kind
Loan excluded as repayable, not a reward

questions.stem_md: Giving reasons, state whether each is included in national income: (i) free medical care given by a factory to its workers; (ii) gifts of money sent by a relative within India; (iii) interest received by a bank on loans to firms.
questions.solution_md: Payment in kind; transfer; factor income for capital.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Included**: it is a reward for work paid in kind, part of compensation of employees.
(ii) **Excluded**: it is a transfer payment; nothing is produced in return.
(iii) **Included**: interest on loans to firms is a factor payment for capital used in production.

questions.stem_md: State three precautions to be taken while estimating national income by the value-added method.
questions.solution_md: Double counting; second-hand goods; self-consumption and imputed rent.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Avoid double counting**: count only value added, not the full value of output of every firm.
2. **Exclude second-hand goods**, but include commissions earned on their sale.
3. **Include production for self-consumption**, such as farm produce kept by farmers, and the **imputed rent** of owner-occupied houses.

questions.stem_md: Unpaid work done at home is left out of national income. Evaluate how this affects comparisons of national income over time in a country where more women are taking paid jobs.
questions.solution_md: Moving work from home to market raises measured income more than real output.

answer.model_answer_md: Unpaid cooking, cleaning and caring are **not counted**. When a woman takes a paid job and the family **hires** help or **buys** prepared food, those services become **market transactions** and enter national income. Part of the measured rise is therefore a **shift of existing work into the market**, not a true rise in production, so growth over time is **overstated**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [3 + 2]

(a) State one precaution for each of the three methods of measuring national income. [3]
(b) Explain two difficulties in measuring national income in India. [2]
questions.solution_md: One precaution per method; two Indian difficulties.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Value-added method**: avoid **double counting** by subtracting intermediate consumption, and include production for self-consumption.
**Income method**: exclude **transfer payments** such as pensions and scholarships, and windfall gains such as lottery prizes.
**Expenditure method**: exclude spending on **second-hand goods** and **financial assets** such as shares, and include only final expenditure, not spending on intermediate goods.
(b) **Non-monetised output**: a large part of output, especially in villages, is kept for self-use or exchanged by barter, and its value has to be guessed. **Inadequate data**: many small producers and self-employed workers keep no accounts and income is often under-reported, so estimates of the informal sector are rough.

questions.stem_md:
In the imagined Mandya sweets chain (₹ crore), cane worth 300 goes to a jaggery unit, jaggery worth 500 goes to a sweet shop, and households buy sweets worth 800. The three firms together pay wages 450, rent 60, interest 90 and profit 200. The grower buys no inputs. [3 + 2]

(a) Measure the chain's output by all three methods. [3]
(b) Explain why the three answers must be the same. [2]
questions.solution_md: Value added, factor incomes and final spending all equal 800; the circular flow explains why.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Value-added method**: 300 + (500 − 300) + (800 − 500) = 300 + 200 + 300 = **₹800 crore**.
**Income method**: 450 + 60 + 90 + 200 = **₹800 crore**.
**Expenditure method**: final spending by households on sweets = **₹800 crore**. Sales of cane and jaggery are intermediate and are not added.
(b) The value added at each stage is **paid out as factor incomes**, so total value added equals total income. That income is **spent** on the final output, so it equals final expenditure. The three methods measure the **same flow** at three points of the circular flow: production, income and spending.

marking_scheme.step: Value added paid out as income

questions.stem_md:
Answer both subparts about the imagined Vidarbha garment unit (₹ lakh). [2 + 2]

(i) It sold garments worth 1,500, added 50 to its stock and bought yarn worth 1,000. Find its gross value added at market price.
(ii) Its depreciation is 40, indirect taxes 45 and subsidy 15. Find its net value added at factor cost.
questions.solution_md: Value of output, gross value added, then net factor-cost value added.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Value of output = 1,500 + 50 = 1,550. Gross value added at market price = 1,550 − 1,000 = **₹550 lakh**, because the yarn is used up in making the garments.
(ii) Net indirect taxes = 45 − 15 = 30. Net value added at factor cost = 550 − 40 − 30 = **₹480 lakh**. Depreciation is removed to make it net, and net indirect taxes to move from market price to factor cost.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Net value added at factor cost

questions.stem_md:
Answer both subparts about imagined Konark (₹ crore). [2 + 2]

(i) Domestic income is 2,600, compensation of employees 1,250, rent 180, interest 140 and mixed income 570. Find profit.
(ii) A survey shows that many self-employed artisans did not report their earnings. Explain how this affects the estimate of profit found in (i).
questions.solution_md: Profit as the remainder; under-reporting shifts income into the remainder.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Profit = 2,600 − 1,250 − 180 − 140 − 570 = **₹460 crore**, the part of domestic income left after the other factor incomes.
(ii) If artisans' earnings are missing, **mixed income is understated**. When domestic income is estimated independently, from output, the remainder shown as **profit is overstated**, because unreported mixed income is wrongly counted as profit. The estimate of profit therefore depends on how complete the other figures are.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both subparts about imagined Shivgarh (₹ crore). [2 + 2]

(i) From private final consumption 960, government final consumption 240, gross domestic capital formation 300, exports 70, imports 90, old-age pensions 30, purchase of shares 55 and purchase of second-hand buses 25, find GDP at market price.
(ii) Give the reason for leaving out each of the last three items.
questions.solution_md: Final expenditure only; reasons for three exclusions.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) GDP at market price = 960 + 240 + 300 + 70 − 90 = **₹1,480 crore**.
(ii) **Old-age pensions** are transfers with nothing produced in return. **Shares** are financial assets; buying them only changes ownership of a claim. **Second-hand buses** were counted in the year they were made, so buying them again adds no new output.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) Explain the value-added method of measuring national income, including the precautions taken.
(ii) For the imagined Mandya sweets chain (₹ crore: cane 300, jaggery 500, sweets 800; wages 450, rent 60, interest 90, profit 200; the grower buys no inputs), show that the value-added and income methods give the same total, and explain what would go wrong if sales were simply added.
questions.solution_md: Method with steps and precautions; equal totals; size of the double counting.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The **value-added method** measures the contribution of each producing unit. Units are grouped into primary, secondary and tertiary sectors. For each, **value of output** (sales plus change in stock) is found, and **intermediate consumption** is subtracted to give gross value added at market price. Adding over all units gives GDP at market price; subtracting depreciation and net indirect taxes and adding net factor income from abroad gives national income. **Precautions**: avoid **double counting**; leave out **second-hand goods** but count commissions on them; include **production for self-consumption** and **imputed rent**.
(ii) Value added = 300 + 200 + 300 = **₹800 crore**. Factor incomes = 450 + 60 + 90 + 200 = **₹800 crore**, the same, because every rupee of value added is paid out as rent, wages, interest or profit. Adding sales gives 300 + 500 + 800 = ₹1,600 crore, which counts the cane twice and the jaggery once more inside the price of sweets: an overstatement of ₹800 crore.

marking_scheme.step: (i) Value of output and value added

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) Imagined Kavalpur (₹ crore) has private final consumption 1,800, government final consumption 400, gross domestic capital formation 500, net exports 60, consumption of fixed capital 120, net indirect taxes 140 and net factor income from abroad 20. Calculate GDP at market price and national income, explaining each adjustment.
(ii) A columnist argues that the expenditure method is the most reliable in a country like India. Evaluate this view.
questions.solution_md: Calculation with reasons for each adjustment; a balanced judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) GDP at market price = 1,800 + 400 + 500 + 60 = **₹2,760 crore**, the total of final spending on domestic output. Subtracting consumption of fixed capital (120) removes the wear and tear of machines; subtracting net indirect taxes (140) moves from market prices to the incomes of factors; adding net factor income from abroad (20) moves from domestic to national. National income = 2,760 − 120 − 140 + 20 = **₹2,520 crore**.
(ii) In favour: big items such as **government spending, investment and trade** are well recorded in budgets, company accounts and customs data. Against: **household consumption** in villages and the informal sector is hard to observe, much output is **kept for self-use**, and spending surveys are occasional. So the method is reliable for the organised parts but not for all. In practice the methods are **used together**, each checking the others, which is more reliable than any one alone.

marking_scheme.step: (i) Net indirect taxes and factor income explained

questions.stem_md: Read the imagined report from the planning board of Tamrapatna and answer the questions that follow. *(Written by SOYL for practice; the country and figures are imagined.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** GDCF = 820 − 40 = 780, that is ₹780 crore.

**(b)** GDP at market price = 3,200 + 650 + 780 + (-50) = 4,580, that is ₹4,580 crore.

**(c) (i)** Transfer; spending already counted.

**OR (c) (ii)** Sales out of old stock are not this year's output.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **780 ₹ crore**

**(b)** **4,580 ₹ crore**

**(c) (i)** Pensions of ₹90 crore are **transfer payments**: no good or service is supplied in return. When pensioners spend them, that spending is **already in household consumption**, so adding the pensions would count it twice.

**OR (c) (ii)** A fall in stocks means some goods sold this year were **produced in earlier years**. Final spending on them is not output of this year, so the **negative change in stock** is included in capital formation and lowers GDP.
